svg.aria-label: Why normals transform by the inverse transpose: under a non-uniform scale, transforming a normal by the same matrix as the surface leaves it no longer perpendicular.
svg.text: a normal is not a direction you can just scale
before
n
perpendicular
after squashing y by half
M · n
(M⁻¹)ᵀ · n
leans — no longer perpendicular
still perpendicular
Scaling the surface tips it one way and the normal the other, so the two
stop being at right angles. The inverse transpose is exactly the matrix that
undoes that. For a rotation it changes nothing, which is why this only bites
once a non-uniform scale shows up.
two places to put the transform
bake it at load
every vertex × M once, when the
model is read. Costs memory and
nothing per ray. What I did.
transform the ray
leave the geometry alone and push
each ray through M⁻¹ instead, then
the hit back through M. Costs a
little per intersection and lets one
mesh appear many times.
I compute the inverse either way.
Baking means the vertices arrive already in world space — so the face normal computed from them is
already correct, and transforming it again would be wrong. The per-hit inverse-transpose line in my
intersection code is left over from the other approach, computed on every hit and never used.
